questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presented with fatigue, subjective fever and chills, and poor appetite. He had a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, and CKD stage 4. He had no known drug allergies. On examination he was found to have a new diastolic murmur. He was started empirically on vancomycin. Investigations: 4/4 blood cultures positive for fully sensitive Enterococcus faecalis Echocardiogram: a 5 mm vegetation of the aortic valve Creatinine clearance 15 mL/min
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone For patients with enterococcal endocarditis with susceptible strains the preferred treatment regimens include ampicillin or penicillin G as these are rapidly cidal agents. For patients with normal renal function these agents should be combined with 2 weeks of aminoglycoside such as gentamicin. In patients with contraindications to aminoglycosides, an alternate regimen of ampicillin and ceftriaxone should be used. Linezolid and daptomycin should be reserved for patients with resistant enterococci not amenable to treatment with rapidly cidal beta-lactams. Vancomycin should be reserved for patients with penicillin-resistant enterococci, and beta-lactams should be used whenever possible. In this patient with a very limited creatinine clearance, vancomycin should also be avoided to prevent further damage to his renal function.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q16

a) Compare banding patterns across the 9 lanes: isolates with identical band patterns are the same clone/strain, indicating a clonal outbreak with patient-to-patient (nosocomial) transmission; lanes differing by only a few bands are closely related subtypes, while those with many band differences are unrelated strains.

questions.model_answer:
a) All enterococci have intrinsic low-level resistance to aminoglycosides, so low-level results are not clinically meaningful; only high-level resistance (HLR) testing predicts whether the synergistic effect with a cell-wall agent is preserved.
b) High-level resistance to both gentamicin and streptomycin abolishes the synergistic bactericidal effect of an aminoglycoside combined with a beta-lactam (or vancomycin); the aminoglycoside can no longer be used for synergy, so a double beta-lactam regimen (ampicillin plus ceftriaxone) should be used instead.
c) Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes: HLR to gentamicin is mostly due to the bifunctional enzyme AAC(6′)-Ie-APH(2″)-Ia; HLR to streptomycin is due to 30S ribosomal subunit mutations or a streptomycin adenylyltransferase.

cohort_answer.text: Only high-level resistance reported: Don't report low-level resistance since all enterococci have intrinsic low-level resistance to aminoglycosides; loss of synergism with beta lactams/vanco if high-level AG resistance present. Therapeutic consequence: Can no longer use AG for synergy with beta-lactam/vanco against enterococcus, if used will lead to clinical failure/higher relapse. Mechanism: AG-modifying enzymes (N-acetylation, O-nucleotidylation, O-phosphorylation) alter the drug so it can no longer bind the 30s ribosome subunit.

questions.model_answer: HLAR: enterococci have intrinsic low-level aminoglycoside resistance; high-level resistance (growth at 500 mg/L gentamicin or 2000 mg/L streptomycin) abolishes the synergistic bactericidal effect with a cell-wall agent. HLR to gentamicin is mediated by the bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6′)-Ie-APH(2″)-Ia, typically carried on mobile genetic elements. Streptomycin: HLR to streptomycin arises by a different mechanism (30S ribosomal mutation or streptomycin adenylyltransferase), so it must be tested separately – gentamicin HLR does NOT predict streptomycin HLR. If the isolate lacks HLR to streptomycin, streptomycin (7.5 mg/kg q12h) can substitute for gentamicin for synergy, with serum-level monitoring given its ototoxicity risk.

questions.model_answer: a) Endocarditis requires bactericidal therapy; beta-lactams alone are not reliably bactericidal against enterococci, but adding gentamicin or streptomycin yields synergistic killing (>=2 log10 fall at 24 h). HLR (growth at 500 mg/L gentamicin or 2000 mg/L streptomycin) abolishes synergy, so HLAR testing is standard of care for endovascular/severe enterococcal infection to decide whether an aminoglycoside is useful. b) No HLR means that aminoglycoside (gentamicin or streptomycin) retains its synergistic bactericidal effect and can be combined with a cell-wall agent. c) High-level gentamicin resistance is chiefly due to the bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2")-Ia; high-level streptomycin resistance is due to 30S ribosomal mutations or a streptomycin adenylyltransferase.

cohort_answer.text: a) Enterococcal endocarditis requires bactericidal regimen but beta-lactams alone aren't readily bactericidal; synergistic bactericidal effect achieved with aminoglycoside addition; synergism = >=2 log10 increase in killing at 24h compared to beta-lactam alone; gentamicin and streptomycin are the two compounds recommended; HLR defined by growth at 2000mg/L streptomycin and 500mg/L gentamicin on BHI agar (or 1000mg/L streptomycin in BHI broth); HLR to both abolishes synergistic effect; evaluation for HLR is standard of care for endovascular/severe enterococcal infections. b) Gentamicin can be used for synergy in endovascular infections. c) Aminoglycoside modifying enzyme (AME) - bifunctional AAC(6')-APH(2'')-Ia confers high level gentamicin resistance due to mutations in 30S ribosomal subunit.

questions.model_answer: a) Class A carbapenemase (enzymatic inactivation), e.g., chromosomal SME (or OXA-48-type), which hydrolyzes carbapenems while sparing extended-spectrum cephalosporins. b) Upregulated efflux (MexAB-OprM) - meropenem is a substrate but imipenem is not; imipenem resistance would instead require OprD porin loss. c) Cell-membrane target alteration (increased net positive surface charge, e.g., mprF), reducing binding of calcium-dependent daptomycin. d) VanC ligase producing D-Ala-D-Ser termini - intrinsic, low-level vancomycin resistance in E. gallinarum with retained teicoplanin susceptibility. e) Derepression/hyperexpression of chromosomal AmpC combined with porin (permeability) loss.

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Carbapenemase (enzyme inactivation) by SME (oxa-48 also can show this pattern). S. aureus/dapto: Target-site alteration (change in bacterial cell membrane composition) - dapto requires calcium to become positively charged and interacts with negatively charged lipid moieties on membrane to kill; increased positive charge on membrane prevents dapto action. E. gallinarum: Target-site alteration - VanC (specific to E. gallinarum); vancomycin binds terminal D-ala-D-ala residues of growing PG cell wall; VanA isolates show high MICs to Vancomycin and Teicoplanin, VanB/VanC often have lower MICs to Vancomycin and are S to Teicoplanin. questions.model_answer: (1) Serratia (carbapenems R, ceftriaxone S): Class A serine carbapenemase - Serratia marcescens enzyme (SME) (chromosomal blaSME); spares cephalosporins. (2) Pseudomonas (Meropenem R, Imipenem S): up-regulated efflux (MexAB-OprM), a meropenem substrate that does not affect imipenem. (3) E. gallinarum (Vancomycin R): intrinsic chromosomal vanC (D-Ala-D-Ser terminus), low-level resistance. (4) E. cloacae (Ceftaz R, Erta R, Cefepime/Mero S): derepressed AmpC (ceftazidime R, cefepime stable) combined with porin (OmpC/OmpF) loss producing ertapenem resistance while meropenem remains active. (5) MRSA (Daptomycin R): mprF mutation increasing membrane positive charge (reduced daptomycin binding). (6) MRSA (Linezolid R): 23S rRNA mutation (G2576T) at the domain V ribosomal target (or cfr methyltransferase).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the E. cloacae AmpC element is grounded in this chapter (p. 2682); SME, Pseudomonas efflux, vanC, and the MRSA mechanisms are established knowledge from Mandell resistance chapters.

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Serratia marcescens enzyme (SME) - carbapenemase Class A. Pseudomonas: MexAB-OprM efflux cassette. E. gallinarum: VanC gene presence (chromosomal). E. cloacae: intrinsic resistance to inducible AmpC (R to beta-lactams); OXA-48 (R to Erta, S to Mero with additional efflux pump or porin). MRSA Daptomycin R: mprF gene (phosphatidylglycerol lysyltransferase). MRSA Linezolid R: 23S RNA G2576T point mutation.

questions.model_answer:
(1) K. pneumoniae/meropenem: carbapenemase production - Ambler class A KPC (most common), class B metallo-beta-lactamases (NDM, VIM, IMP), class D OXA-48-type; also ESBL/AmpC plus porin loss (OmpK35/OmpK36).
(2) P. aeruginosa/meropenem: loss/downregulation of the OprD porin (with basal AmpC); acquired metallo-beta-lactamases (VIM, IMP); upregulated MexAB-OprM efflux (affects mero/dori but not imipenem).
(3) E. faecium/penicillin: overproduction of a low-affinity penicillin-binding protein PBP5 (altered target).
(4) E. faecalis/high-level aminoglycoside resistance: acquired aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme, classically the bifunctional AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2'')-Ia.
(5) S. pneumoniae/moxifloxacin: stepwise target mutations in the quinolone-resistance-determining regions of gyrA (DNA gyrase) and parC (topoisomerase IV).
(6) S. pyogenes/erythromycin: ribosomal methylation of 23S rRNA by an erm-encoded methylase (MLSB phenotype), or macrolide efflux via mef.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mechanisms are from Mandell Ch. 18 (antimicrobial resistance) / standard microbiology, not this Enterobacteriaceae chapter.

cohort_answer.text: K. pneumoniae/Meropenem: Ambler class D oxacillinases (OXAs); acquired class B beta-lactamases (VIM, NDM); Ambler Class A KPCs; reduced expression of OmpK35/OmpK36. P. aeruginosa/Meropenem: downregulated/absent OprD porin with background AmpC; MBLs (VIM, IMP, SPM-1 less common); upregulation of MexA-MexB-OprM efflux (resistant to mero/doripenem but not imipenem). E. faecium/Penicillin: altered PBPs (resistant pbp5 allele). E. faecalis/HLAR: bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-IE-APH(2'')-Ia. S. pneumoniae/Moxifloxacin: dual mutations in GyrA and ParC. S. pyogenes/Erythromycin: erm gene (ribosome methylation) - methylase enzymes dimethylate adenine on 23S rRNA of 50S subunit, disrupting MLS binding.

questions.model_answer: a) VanA-type resistance: acquisition of the vanA gene cluster reprograms peptidoglycan precursor synthesis so terminal D-Ala-D-Ala is replaced by D-Ala-D-Lac, drastically lowering glycopeptide binding; this confers high-level vancomycin resistance with cross-resistance to teicoplanin. b) Not covered in this chapter - typically plasmid-mediated multidrug resistance (e.g., an IncH1 plasmid carrying ampicillin, chloramphenicol, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole resistance). c) Not covered in this chapter - chromosomal (often derepressed) AmpC beta-lactamase, an Ambler class C cephalosporinase.
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts b (Salmonella plasmid-mediated resistance) and c (Enterobacter AmpC class C cephalosporinase) are general microbiology, not in this Enterococcus chapter.

cohort_answer.text: A) VanA gene acquisition - mediates high level vanco resistance by target modification to D-ala-D-lac; most common type, usually higher level resistance, cross-resistance to teicoplanin. B) Incompatible (Inc) plasmids - IncH1 plasmid acquisition leads to concurrent resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, TMP/SMX. C) Class C - AmpC beta-lactamase (chromosomal).
